title: Expected Value & Fair Games
relevance: SDE and quant OAs/interviews use EV, linearity, optional stopping, and waiting-time problems to test probabilistic reasoning under dependence and decision rules.
company_notes: Optiver is named on a fair-coin restart-on-tails fair-value game; trading interviews also ask market-making quotes centered on EV.

phases.goal: Establish EV, fair price, and linearity—including that independence is not required.

must_hit.point: For a discrete random variable X, E[X] equals the sum of each outcome times its probability; a game is fair when expected net profit is zero, so the fair price equals expected payoff.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the sum x_i P(X=x_i) definition and equates fair price with expected payoff / zero expected net profit.

must_hit.point: Linearity of expectation holds for any random variables, even when they are dependent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly says E[sum X_i] = sum E[X_i] without needing independence.

must_hit.point: For complex expected totals, decompose into indicator variables X_i in {0, 1} and sum the individual E[X_i].
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions breaking the total into 0-1 indicators and adding their expectations.

must_hit.point: The fair price to play a game that pays the face of a fair 6-sided die is 3.5.

probes: What is expected value, when is a game fair, and does linearity of expectation require independence?

hints.1: Start from the discrete sum definition and what zero expected net profit means.
hints.2: State linearity for a sum, then say whether dependence breaks it.
hints.3: E[X]=sum x_i P(X=x_i); fair price = expected payoff; linearity holds even if variables are dependent—use indicators for totals.

phases.goal: Show how to compute EV via conditioning, optional stopping thresholds, geometric waits, and coupon collecting.

must_hit.point: With one optional reroll on a fair 6-sided die, keep 4, 5, or 6 and reroll 1, 2, or 3; the game EV is 4.25.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Works backwards from second-roll EV 3.5, keeps faces above that threshold, and gets 4.25.

must_hit.point: Expected fair-coin flips until the first Heads is 2; until HH is 6; until HT is 4.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives geometric 1/p = 2 for first Heads, then state/recursion answers 6 for HH and 4 for HT.

must_hit.point: Coupon collector on a fair 6-sided die: expected rolls to see all faces is 14.7.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes sum of geometrics E[T_k]=6/(7-k) and totals 14.7.

must_hit.point: For non-negative integer-valued X, E[X] equals the sum over k≥1 of P(X≥k); conditioning gives E[X] as a mixture of conditional expectations over states.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites the tail-sum identity and the E[X]=sum P(state)·E[X|state] recursion form.

probes: How do you find the EV of a die game with optional rerolls, and the expected flips to get HH versus HT?

hints.1: For rerolls, decide keep vs reroll by comparing the face to the EV of rolling again.
hints.2: For patterns, set up states for the current streak and write equations by conditioning on the next flip.
hints.3: One reroll: keep ≥4 → EV 4.25; first Heads → 2; HH → 6; HT → 4; six faces → 14.7.

phases.goal: Separate EV pricing from variance, risk preference, streak-structure effects, and heavy-tailed means.

must_hit.point: Two games can share expected return 100 while Var(A)=0 and Var(B)=10000, so risk-averse vs risk-seeking choices diverge even when EVs match.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts sure $100 with a coin flip $200/$0, cites variances 0 and 10000, and links preference to risk attitude.

must_hit.point: In quant interviews, games are priced on EV (risk-neutral) unless specified otherwise, but variance still matters for position sizing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says price on expected value by default, then notes variance for sizing.

must_hit.point: HH and HT each have probability 1/4 in two flips, but expected waiting times differ because failure modes leave different residual progress.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects equal-wait intuition; HT failure via HH still leaves an H, while HH failure via HT resets.

must_hit.point: St. Petersburg has infinite expected payout, yet people will not pay a large fee—EV alone is a poor guide for heavy-tailed payoffs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States divergent sum of 1s, then cites utility/bankroll reasons EV misleads.

probes: If two games have the same EV, when would you still prefer one—and why can HH and HT waits differ?

hints.1: Compare not just means but how payoffs are spread and how streaks reset.
hints.2: Name variance/risk preference for equal-EV games, and residual state for pattern waits.
hints.3: Game A variance 0 vs Game B 10000; risk-neutral EV pricing; HH wait 6 vs HT wait 4; St. Petersburg EV infinite.

phases.goal: Apply linearity, martingales, market-making, and classic stopping rules to interview-style problems.

must_hit.point: In the hat-check problem, expected fixed points is 1 for any N, via indicators each with probability 1/N.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines X_i for person i, gets N·(1/N)=1 independent of N.

must_hit.point: Expected left-to-right records in a random permutation of N distinct numbers is the harmonic number H_N.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses P(record at i)=1/i and sums to H_N.

must_hit.point: Fair gambler's ruin from A with barriers 0 and N: probability of hitting N is A/N; expected steps until absorption is A(N-A).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses martingale/constant expected wealth for A/N and the parabola A(N-A) for duration.

must_hit.point: Market on the sum of 100 fair 6-sided dice should center at 350; secretary look-then-leap skips about the first 37% and succeeds about 37% for large n.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Quotes EV 100×3.5=350 as midpoint; states ≈n/e cutoff and 1/e≈37% success.

probes: What is the expected number of fixed hats, and how would you make a market on the sum of 100 dice?

hints.1: Reach for indicators or linearity before enumerating permutations.
hints.2: For ruin, equate starting wealth to expected terminal wealth; for markets, center on EV.
hints.3: Hats → 1; records → H_N; ruin → A/N and A(N-A); 100 dice → 350; secretary → ~37% skip and ~37% win.

tradeoffs.topic: Equal EV vs variance / risk preference
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Game A sure $100 and Game B coin-flip $200/$0 both have E[X]=100, but Var(A)=0 while Var(B)=10000; risk-averse prefers A, risk-seeking prefers B. Quant pricing defaults to risk-neutral EV, with variance used for position sizing.

tradeoffs.topic: HH vs HT expected waiting time
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both patterns have probability 1/4 in two flips, but waits are not equal: failing HH via HT fully resets, while failing HT via HH leaves an H in progress—so E[HH]=6 and E[HT]=4.

tradeoffs.topic: EV pricing vs heavy-tailed / divergent expectations
tradeoffs.strong_answer: St. Petersburg has infinite EV because each term is 1, yet no one pays a huge fee; diminishing utility and finite bankrolls mean variance and ruin risk—not EV alone—should drive decisions when the mean is dominated by rare outcomes.

gotchas.trap: Assuming HH and HT have the same expected waiting time because each has probability 1/4 in two flips.
gotchas.correction: Failure leaves different states: HT after aiming for HH resets completely; HH while aiming for HT still leaves an H—so expected waits are 6 vs 4.

gotchas.trap: Treating a divergent or heavy-tailed expectation (e.g. St. Petersburg) as a practical fair price.
gotchas.correction: An infinite or rare-event-dominated mean is a warning: variance and ruin risk should drive the decision, not EV alone.

gotchas.trap: Quoting a market whose midpoint is off the true EV (e.g. 340 @ 345 when the sum of 100 dice has EV 350).
gotchas.correction: Center the bid/ask on EV (350); a mispriced ask lets the interviewer buy and lock in positive EV against you.

gotchas.trap: Thinking linearity of expectation requires independence.
gotchas.correction: Linearity always holds; dependence does not block summing E[X_i], which is why indicator decompositions work on dependent events like hat checks and adjacent aces.
